claims.text: The moderate hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are governed by the extent of short-range chemical ordering in its simple solid-solution state.
Short-range ordered clusters act as localized obstacles to dislocation motion.
Short-range ordering modestly increases hardness and yield strength.
The short-range ordered state retains ductility because enough slip systems remain available.
Conventionally cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can be prepared as a single-phase simple solid solution.
Rapid quenching minimizes short-range-order formation in CoCrFeNiTi.
Annealing promotes short-range-order formation in CoCrFeNiTi.
Annealing at approximately 800 °C for one hour is an appropriate treatment for promoting short-range ordering.
Annealing produces short-range ordered atomic clusters that impede dislocation glide.
Increasing short-range order raises hardness and yield strength by increasing local obstacles to dislocation motion.
Limited short-range order in as-cast or rapidly quenched material permits easier slip propagation.
Easier slip propagation causes lower strength and hardness and higher ductility.
Relative to rapidly quenched samples, annealed samples with promoted short-range order will have higher hardness and compressive or tensile strength.
Relative to rapidly quenched samples, annealed samples with promoted short-range order will have lower plasticity.
The predicted mechanical effects of short-range order should be observable at room temperature and around 600 °C.
Untreated equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in the simple solid-solution state has moderate hardness and strength and favorable ductility and machinability.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when significant secondary phases, segregation, or other processing-induced microstructural features are present.
Transmission electron microscopy or atom-probe tomography can assess the extent and spatial distribution of short-range order in these samples.
